1 Course Map and How to Use This Document
This document is a complete, self-contained companion for weeks 5–7 of the Foun-
dation course English for Engineering - I at Tashkent University of Technology (Fall
2026, 4 ECTS; module coordinators Ella Tsoy and Florence Dujarric, Faculty of En-
ergy Engineering). The module is mandatory for all Bachelor of Science tracks —
60 classroom hours (30 lecture +30 practical) plus 60 hours of independent study,
with no prerequisites or co-requisites — and it prepares Foundation students to move
from general school English to confident, accurate and organized everyday and aca-
demic communication. This companion was compiled by hand from every relevant
course file for the block: the Week 5, Week 6 and Week 7 lecture decks and the Week
5 grammar worksheet (the passive and its uses). The Week 5–6 files are image scans
transcribed by OCR, and obvious scanning artifacts have been cleaned, but every
question, gap-fill, matching task, definition and discussion prompt that appears in
those sources is reproduced word-for-word, and every exercise is followed by a full
answer key. Under the syllabus assessment table, Test 2, which covers this block, is
a paper-based writing task (1 hour, 10 %), so the grammar catalogues below receive
the most detailed treatment.
The scope follows the official course structure. Week 5 opens the block with the topic
Describing Processes and Sequences: the grammar strand is the passive (all tenses),
previewed through the TED talk The solution to our energy problems. . . is a toaster;
the lecture then works through the manufacturing-process vocabulary (drilling, cast-
ing, welding. . .), the reading How Is Tea Made?, and a describing-a-process strand
built around a solar-radiation text and its sequencing language.
Week 6 turns to
Understanding Graphs and Short Talks: the oral-expression strand trains describing
simple graphs and charts (diagram types, movement verbs and nouns, adjective and
adverb pairs), the lecture adds cause-and-effect language and a listening strand on
the structure and signposting of short talks, plus the TED talk How to Spot a Mis-
leading Graph. Week 7 closes the block with Comparing Solutions: the grammar
strand is noun formation — introduced with the word formation video «Virtually Flu-
ent» and worked through suffixes, prefixes, roots, compound nouns and conversion
— followed by reading comprehension and the Switch Games oral expression.
Each weekly part of this document has the same internal structure. First comes the
rules catalogue: every rule, form table and language box that the week’s sources
teach, written out formally and numbered continuously so that any rule can be cited
from the answer keys. Then come the questions and tasks, grouped exactly as they
appear in the source files, each tagged with its source and followed immediately by a
complete answer key. Listening and video activities are reproduced with their tasks;
where an answer depends on a recording or an image page that only students in class
can see, the key marks the expected answer type and the most probable completion,
so the exercise can still be checked. The appendix at the end collects quick-reference
material — a passive quick reference, a graph language bank of verb + preposition
patterns, a noun formation table and ten one-line revision answers — so that the
question bank here is complete «to the end».

2.2 Grammar catalogue for Week 5
[Source: Week 5 Lecture (ew5lec.txt), Part 1 — Language Reference: passive (all tenses); Week 5
Grammar Worksheet
(ew5gw.txt), rules page «the passive and its uses»]
Week 5 has one grammar block: the passive, in all the tenses the course needs for
describing processes and sequences. The rules below collect the language-reference
panel of the Week 5 lecture and the complete rules page of the Week 5 grammar
worksheet; every example is quoted from the two files.
• Form. We often use the passive (be + past participle) when it isn’t said, known,
or important who
does an action: A lot of films are shot on location. The director died when the film
was being made. When is our car being repaired? You’ll be picked up at the airport
by one of our staff. This bill must be paid tomorrow. I love being given a massage.
The new concert hall will be opened by the King. In passive sentences, the object of
the verb becomes the new subject: Artem’s bike has been stolen. (= somebody has
stolen Artem’s bike, but we don’t know who.)
• Use of the passive (worksheet rules page). Use the passive (a) to move important
information —
the object of the active sentence — to the beginning of the sentence: Two men are
being questioned by the police.; (b) to be impersonal and not mention the name of
the person who performs the action
• we often use the passive in scientific or technical processes: Oil and gas are
found beneath the ground or sea; (c) when it is obvious who performed the
action (e.g. teachers), or when we do not want to use a general subject such

as people, they: Aztec boys were trained to fight. Two missing children have
been found safe and well.; (d) more often in formal speech and writing than in
everyday speech.
• The agent by. If we want to say who did the action, we use by (lecture). Use by
when it is
important to know the «agent» or person who performed the action — Some countries
have been harmed by tourism. Many buildings in the city have been damaged by the
earthquake. — and only when it is really necessary: The two men were arrested. (by
the police — this is obvious).
• Active or passive — two ways of focusing. We can often say things in two ways,
in the active or
in the passive. Compare: Napoleon was directed by Ridley Scott. (= we want to
focus more on the film) / Ridley Scott directed Napoleon. (= we want to focus more
on the director).
• Negatives and questions are formed in the same way as in active sentences:
Some films aren’t shot
on location. Is your car being repaired today?
• Present simple passive: am/is/are + past participle (for processes that are gen-
erally true): Oil
and gas are found beneath the ground or sea. This room isn’t used very often. Past
simple passive: was/were + past participle (for finished events): The college was
built in the 16th century. Aztec boys were trained to fight.
• Transitive and intransitive verbs. Verbs which have an object are called transi-
tive verbs; verbs
without an object are intransitive. Only transitive verbs can be made passive: I lost
my wallet on the way to school. (transitive) / I swim every day. (intransitive).
• The preposition with. Use with for objects which perform actions: The game
was played with a
ball of solid rubber.
• The passive in science and engineering. We often use the passive to talk about
processes,
because the steps of the process matter more than the person doing them: the man-
ufacturing descriptions of the lecture are all passive — A hole is made using a drill.
A material is pressed into the correct shape. Hot liquid material is poured into a con-
tainer and cooled. . . — and the same pattern runs through the week’s science text:
Around 25% is then reflected by the upper atmosphere and clouds. . . Finally, 50% is
absorbed by the Earth’s surface.

• Sequencing a process. There are a number of different ways to talk about events
in a process. You
can use adverbs — firstly, then, next, after that, finally (Firstly, some energy is re-
moved by the clouds.). You can also use words like after, as, as soon as, once and
when to show how two events relate to each other (As soon as sunlight hits the flower,
its petals open.). The phrase at this stage is used to help create a clear sequence (The
temperature reaches 100°C. At this stage, the water in the container begins to boil.).
Tense Active Passive
present simple We find oil and gas beneath the ground or sea. Oil and gas are found
beneath the ground or sea.
present continuous The police are questioning two men. Two men are being ques-
tioned by the police.
past simple Teachers trained Aztec boys to fight. Aztec boys were trained to fight.
present perfect Tourism has harmed some countries.
Some countries have been
harmed by tourism.
will We will choose a new class representative on A new class representative will be
chosen on Monday. Monday.

2.2.1 Preview activities — TED talk «The solution to our energy problems. . .
is a toaster»
Before listening, the lecture previews the key vocabulary of the talk in three panels.
Learn each term together with its definition and the way it is used in the talk — the
definitions are the answers.
Environmental & Energy Terms
Preview 1 — Fossil Fuels (noun). Give the definition and the example from
the talk.
Answer.
Definition: natural energy sources formed from the remains of ancient
plants and animals (such as coal, oil, and natural gas). In this talk: most industrial
manufacturers burn fossil fuels to create high-temperature heat.
Preview 2 — Carbon Pollution / Emissions (noun). Give the definition and the
example from the talk.
Answer. Definition: greenhouse gases (mostly CO₂) released into the atmosphere
that trap heat and damage the climate. In this talk: industrial heat is responsible for
roughly 20% of global carbon pollution.
Preview 3 — Intermittent (adjective).
Give the definition and the example
from the talk.
Answer. Definition: not continuous; stopping and starting at irregular intervals. In
this talk: renewable energy from wind and solar is intermittent because it depends
on the weather (the wind blowing or the sun shining).
Materials & Mechanical Terms
5

English for Engineering I — Weeks 5–7
Rules · Questions · Answers
Preview 4 — Composite (noun). Give the definition and the example from the
talk.
Answer. Definition: a material made by combining two or more distinct elements to
create a new substance with improved properties. In this talk: a nickel and chromium
composite was invented in 1905 to make better heating elements.
Preview 5 — Filament / Heating Element (noun). Give the definition and the
example from the talk.
Answer. Definition: a thin wire or metal piece that converts electricity into thermal
energy (heat) due to electrical resistance. In this talk: the large storage bricks are
threaded with filaments, just like the ones inside a kitchen toaster.
Preview 6 — Abundant (adjective). Give the definition and the example from
the talk.
Answer. Definition: available in large quantities; plentiful and easy to find. In this
talk: materials like bricks, rocks, and molten salt are cheap and abundant, making
them great for storing heat.
Thermal & Structural Terms
Preview 7 — Disperse (verb). Give the definition and the example from the
talk.
Answer. Definition: to scatter, spread out, or distribute something evenly over a wide
area. In this talk: coiled toaster wires allow heat to be dispersed evenly across a slice
of bread or a structural brick.
Preview 8 — Encased (adjective/verb). Give the definition and the example
from the talk.
Answer. Definition: completely enclosed, covered, or wrapped in a protective con-
tainer or outer layer. In this talk: the entire thermal battery system is encased in
insulating steel.
Preview 9 — Insulation (noun). Give the definition and the example from the
talk.
Answer. Definition: a material used to trap heat, electricity, or sound and prevent
it from escaping. In this talk: steel insulation ensures that less than 1% of the heat
escapes the battery chamber daily.
Preview 10 — Channels (noun). Give the definition and the example from the
talk.
Answer. Definition: narrow, open pathways or passages through which air, gas, or
liquids can flow. In this talk: the interlocking blocks are molded with open channels
so that cold gases can be blown through them to collect the stored heat.

2.2.3 Listening for gist
Choose the best answer for each question.
Listening for gist 1.
What is the main topic of this TED-Ed talk?
A) The
history of kitchen appliances and how they changed breakfast. B) Using a
century-old toaster technology to build large-scale heat batteries for indus-
try. C) The process of manufacturing high-quality bricks, rocks, and molten
salt. D) How wind and solar energy can completely replace the electric grid
today.
Answer. B) Using a century-old toaster technology to build large-scale heat batter-
ies for industry. The talk explains how the heating element of a toaster — a nickel
and chromium composite invented in 1905 — is now threaded through cheap, abun-
dant storage bricks so that intermittent renewable energy can be stored as heat for
industry.
Listening for gist 2. Why is industrial heat a major environmental problem
according to the talk? A) It consumes over 80% of the world’s fresh water
supply. B) It is too expensive for small companies to generate safely. C) Most
companies burn fossil fuels to achieve high temperatures, creating 20% of
global carbon pollution.
D) Industrial factories release too much hot air
directly into the atmosphere, causing global warming.
Answer. C) Most companies burn fossil fuels to achieve high temperatures, creat-
ing 20% of global carbon pollution. The glossary line confirms it: industrial heat is
responsible for roughly 20% of global carbon pollution.

Activity 1 — answer key (10 items).
Answer. (1) are being made; (2) inspired — the story performs the action, so the

active; (10) was taken. Rule of thumb: choose the passive when the subject under-
goes the action and the doer is unknown or unimportant (Rules 1–2); keep the active
when the subject performs the action on an object (Rule 7).

Activity 2 — answer key (10 items).
Answer. (1) A lot of foreign films are subtitled. (2) Love in the Time of Cholera was
written in 1985. (3) My laptop is being repaired at the moment. (4) The DVD of the

2.3.2 Task 2 — a manufacturing process (check valve)
1 Look at the diagrams. Listen to the description of the manufacturing process for a
check valve. Number the steps in the correct order. (The six diagrams of the lecture
show bolting, drilling, turning, inspection, casting and painting.) — The numbering
depends on the recording; from the diagrams and the descriptions the expected order
follows the manufacturing logic: the body of the valve is cast, then turned on a lathe,
then the holes are drilled, the parts are bolted together, the valve is painted, and
finally the work is inspected.
2 Listen again. Answer the questions.
Task 2, question 1.
What verb tense does the speaker use to explain the
process?
Answer. The present simple passive — is/are + past participle (Rule 6): a hole is
made, a surface is covered, the pieces are joined. . .
Task 2, question 2. Why is this tense used?
Answer.
Because in a manufacturing process it is the steps that matter, not the
person who performs them: who does the action is not said, known or important
(Rule 1), and the passive is the standard way of describing scientific and technical
processes (Rules 2 and 9).
Task 2, question 3. What words does the speaker use to explain the order of
the steps in the process?
Answer. Sequencing words: first(ly), then, next, after that, finally — the adverbs of
the sequencing box (Rule 10).
2.3.3 Speaking — explaining a manufacturing process
Work in pairs. Student A uses handout A, and student B uses handout B to explain
a manufacturing process. (The handouts are distributed in class; the model below
shows the expected style.)
Speaking task — model answer.
Answer. A full description uses the present simple passive plus sequencing words:
First, the body of the valve is cast from hot metal and cooled to make the correct
shape. Then it is turned on a lathe, and part of the material is removed. Next, a hole
is drilled, and the parts are bolted together with a nut and a bolt. After that, the
valve is painted. Finally, the work is checked carefully — the valve is inspected.

2.4.2 Activity 2: True or false?
Read the article. Write T (true) or F (false) for each statement. If a statement is

Rules · Questions · Answers
• Tea factories are usually far from the tea gardens.
• Only 24 hours pass between plucking the leaves and packing the tea.
• The withering stage takes only a few minutes.
• During oxidation, the leaves change colour from green to brown.
• In China, teas are always named after the person who made them.
• CTC tea was invented to increase the weight of tea that could be packed into a
sack.
• Oolong tea is made from fully oxidised leaves.
• Green tea is made without the oxidation stage.
Activity 2 — answer key (8 statements).
Answer. (1) F — tea factories are usually built close to the tea gardens, so that the
leaves can be processed quickly after plucking (see Activity 3, question 1). (2) T
— the whole process from plucking to packing takes about 24 hours. (3) F — the
withering stage takes several hours: the leaves lose their moisture and become soft
and weak (definition G), not a few minutes. (4) T — during oxidation the leaves react
with the air and change colour from green to brown (definition D). (5) F — teas are
not always named after the person who made them; many are named after other
things, such as the place where they are made. (6) T — CTC tea is crushed, torn and
curled into small granules, so more tea fits into a sack. (7) F — oolong tea is made
from partially oxidised leaves. (8) T — green tea is made without the oxidation stage
(see Activity 3, question 6).
2.4.3 Activity 3: Short answers
Answer each question in one or two full sentences, using your own words where you
can.
Activity 3, question 1. Why are tea factories usually built close to the tea
gardens?
Answer. Because the leaves must be processed very soon after plucking; if the fac-
tories were far away, the leaves would lose their moisture and quality on the way.
Activity 3, question 2. Why are the leaves separated into batches of the same
size?
Answer. So that all the leaves in a batch are processed in the same way: leaves of
the same size wither, roll and oxidize evenly, which gives a consistent, well-graded
tea.
Activity 3, question 3. What are the four stages of the orthodox method?
Answer. Withering, rolling, oxidation and drying — after drying, the tea is graded
and packed.
Activity 3, question 4. What happens to the leaves during oxidation, and what
does this stage decide?
Answer. During oxidation the enzymes inside the leaves react with the air, and the
leaves change colour from green to brown and develop their flavour.
This stage
decides the type and strength of the tea — how dark and strong it will be.
12


English for Engineering I — Weeks 5–7
Rules · Questions · Answers
Activity 3, question 5. How is the CTC method different from the orthodox
method of rolling?
Answer. In the orthodox method the leaves are rolled into twisted pieces, but in the
CTC method the leaves are crushed, torn and curled by machines into small granules;
the process is faster, and the granules pack more tea into a sack.
Activity 3, question 6. Why does green tea have a light, fresh flavour?
Answer.
Because green tea is made without the oxidation stage: the leaves are
heated so that the enzymes stop working, and the leaves keep their light, fresh
flavour.

2.5.1 Text A — solar radiation (model text with glossary and usage note)
The model text of the strand (adapted from Johnson, K. (2016). GCSE Physics For
You. (5th ed.). Oxford: Oxford University Press, p. 214): All the planets absorb heat
from the sun in a process known as solar radiation. However, for life on our planet
to continue, Earth must stay at an average surface temperature of around 15°C. For
the Earth to stay at a constant temperature, it needs to absorb and emit radiation at
the same rates. As solar radiation travels to Earth, there is a series of steps which
reduce the amount of radiation that reaches the surface: firstly, some is removed as
it enters the atmosphere — the mixture of gases that surround our planet. Around
25% is then reflected by the upper atmosphere and clouds, while a further 20% is
absorbed by them. 5% of the radiation is reflected from the surface of the Earth —
by deserts or ice. Finally, 50% is absorbed by the Earth’s surface. Around 10% of
this heat radiates from the surface, and the remaining 40% moves to the clouds and
atmosphere. This heat is then radiated back out into space, completing the cycle.
Glossary: absorb (v): to take in and keep heat, light, or other forms of energy; emit
(v): to send out light or heat; reflect (v): to send back light or heat from a surface
(the third definition line is only partly legible in the scan).
Usage note — sequence in a process (verbatim): There are a number of different
ways to talk about events in a process. You can use adverbs: firstly, then, next, after
that, finally — Firstly, some energy is removed by the clouds. You can also use words
like after, as, as soon as, once and when to show how two events relate to each other
— As soon as sunlight hits the flower, its petals open. The phrase at this stage is used

3.1.1 Diagram types
• Diagrams are visual ways of presenting data concisely. They are often also called
figures. In an
academic article they are usually labelled Fig. (Figure) 1, Fig. 2, etc.
• A pie chart is a circle divided into segments from the middle (like slices of a
cake) to show how
the total is divided up. A key or legend shows what each segment represents.

• A bar chart is a diagram in which different amounts are represented by thin
vertical or horizontal
bars which have the same width but vary in height or length.
• A histogram is a kind of bar chart but the bar width also varies to indicate dif-
ferent values.
• A table is a grid with columns and rows of numbers.
• A cross-section is something, or a model of something, cut across the middle so
that you can see
the inside.
A cross-section of the earth’s crust, for example, shows the different
layers that make it up.
A label gives the name of each part of the cross-section.
Cross-section can also be used to mean a small group that is representative of all the
different types within the total group (e.g. the survey looked at a cross-section of
society).
• A flowchart is a diagram which indicates the stages of a process.
• Common mistake. Don’t use the definite article (the) when referring to a specific
diagram: See
Table 4 (NOT See the Table 4).
3.1.2 Graph language: axes, points and lines
• Graphs are drawn by plotting points on them and then drawing a line to join
adjacent points. If
there are two separate lines on a graph, the lines can cross or intersect at various
points. Lines that run parallel to one another never intersect.
• Line charts and bar charts have a vertical axis and a horizontal axis; each axis
is labelled to
indicate what type of information it contains. Typical information included on the
vertical and horizontal axis: age — how old; weight — how heavy; height — how tall;
date — which day, month, year, etc.; time — how much time is required; length —
how long; width — how wide; degrees — how hot or cold; percentage — a portion of
100%; number; duration — the length of time required.
• Model description (the lecture’s pocket-money example): The graph presents
data relating to
teenagers and pocket money. A random sample of 1,000 teenagers were surveyed
and the average pocket money received at each age has been plotted on the graph.
The x axis or horizontal axis indicates age and the y axis or vertical axis shows the
amount of money received per week.
The graph shows that 15-year-olds receive
twice as much pocket money as 13-year-olds. From the graph we can see that the
amount received reaches a peak at the age of 18 and then starts to decline. This
decline can perhaps be explained by the fact that many teenagers start earning and
stop receiving pocket money at the age of 18.

fall, drop or decline. Other verbs used about growth include double, soar, multiply,

amount; opposite = halve; soar = increase very quickly and by a large amount; oppo-

decrease, are followed by in (to explain what is rising) or of (to explain the size of

to rise — a rise;
to improve — an improvement; to recover — a recovery; to increase — an increase.

3.1.7 Short talk structure and signposting language
When listening to a lecture, you need to be able to recognize the main points and
supporting details. It is also important to understand how information and ideas are
organized. Lecturers may use signposting expressions to show how their lecture will
be organized — recognizing these expressions will help you understand what you
are going to hear and the order in which you will hear it. Lectures also often include
definitions and explanations of key terms and ideas; it is important to recognize these
in order to take effective notes. A short talk has three visible parts: the introduction
(giving an overview), the main points (sequenced one by one) and the conclusion.

4.1.2 Conversion — complete rules (verbatim from the lecture)
What is conversion? Conversion means that a word changes its job without changing
its shape. We add no prefix and no suffix. The same word simply starts to work as a
different part of speech. • water (noun): Can I have a glass of water? • water (verb):
Please water the plants. Compare this with the roots method. There, we add pieces
to a root: inspect →inspector →inspection. In conversion, we add nothing: an email
→to email. Teachers sometimes call this «zero derivation», because the ending is
zero. Conversion is very common in English. It is one reason why English learners
can use new words quickly: if you know the noun, you can often guess the verb.
Common patterns. The most common change is from a noun to a verb. Verb to noun
is also very frequent.
Pattern Word Before After
noun →verb email I got an email. Email me tomorrow.
noun →verb phone My phone is new. I’ll phone you tonight.
noun →verb book I’m reading a book. We booked a table.
noun →verb brush Use a brush. Brush your teeth.
verb →noun run I run every day. I went for a run.

verb →noun drink I drink tea. Would you like a drink?
verb →noun smile She smiled at me. She has a lovely smile.
verb →noun help Can you help me? Thanks for your help.
adjective →verb clean The room is clean. Please clean the room.
adjective →verb empty The box is empty. Empty the box.
adjective →verb calm He stayed calm. Calm down!
adjective →noun the rich, the a rich man The rich do not always feel happy. young
With the + adjective, the word means a group of people: the poor, the old, the young,
the unemployed. It takes a plural verb: The young are often good with technology.
How to tell which word you have. Because the shape does not change, the sentence
tells you the job of the word. Ask three questions: 1. Where is it? After a, the, my,
some or an adjective, it is a noun: a drink, my phone, some help. After a subject or
after to, will, can, must, it is a verb: I drink tea. I will phone you. 2. Can it change
form? A verb can take -s, -ed, -ing: she emails, she emailed, she is emailing.
A noun takes a/an or a plural -s: an email, two emails. 3. Does the stress move? A
small group of two-syllable words change stress. The noun has stress on the first
syllable, and the verb on the second.
Noun Verb

A few words also change the final sound: a use /juːs/ →to use /juːz/; a house /haʊs/ →
to house /haʊz/.
Watch out. • The meaning changes a little. When a noun becomes a verb, the new
meaning is usually one of three types: put in or on (to butter bread = put butter on
it), use (to phone someone = use a phone), or act as (to chair a meeting = be the
chair). • Not every word converts. We say to email but not to computer. There is no
rule. When you meet a new word, check a dictionary: it lists every job the word can
do. • New conversions appear all the time: to google (search online), to zoom (have
a video call), to ghost (stop answering someone), to bookmark (save a page). Many
are informal, so check the style before you use them in an essay. • Do not confuse
conversion with suffixes. Advice (noun) and advise (verb) are different words with
different spelling. That is not conversion.

Revision 1. How do you form the present simple passive?
Answer. With am/is/are + past participle — This room isn’t used very often.
Revision 2. How do you form the past simple passive?
Answer. With was/were + past participle — The college was built in the 16th century.

Answer. When it is important to know the agent — Some countries have been harmed
